letters.name: gamma
letters.koine: g as in go; y before front vowels

letters.name: eta
letters.confusion: Looks like Latin n — but it is a vowel, “ē” (Erasmian) or “i” (restored Koine).

letters.name: nu
letters.confusion: Looks like Latin v — it is an “n” sound.

letters.name: xi
letters.confusion: The “ks” sound is this letter, not χ — χ is the one that looks like Latin x, and it is “kh.”

letters.name: rho
letters.confusion: Looks like Latin p — it is an “r” sound.

letters.name: sigma
letters.erasmian: s as in sit (final form ς)
letters.koine: s as in sit (final form ς)

letters.name: chi
letters.confusion: Looks like Latin x — but it is “kh”, not “ks”. The “ks” sound is ξ.

letters.name: omega
letters.confusion: Looks like Latin w — it is an “o” sound.

diacritics.title: Breathings
diacritics.body: Every word starting with a vowel or ρ carries a smooth breathing (silent) or a rough breathing (adds /h/) over the first vowel — or the second, in a diphthong.

diacritics.title: Accents
diacritics.body: Acute, grave, circumflex. They mark an ancient pitch change, not stress. Learn to recognise them, not to reproduce them: you can read and parse correctly without them.

diacritics.title: Iota subscript
diacritics.body: A small ι written under α, η or ω — a former diphthong, now silent. It still matters for parsing: it is part of some dative endings.

diacritics.title: Diaeresis
diacritics.body: Over ι or υ, marking that it starts a new syllable rather than forming a diphthong with the vowel before it (Ἠσαΐας).

diacritics.title: Punctuation
diacritics.body: A raised dot is the semicolon/colon; a semicolon is the question mark — the opposite of English. Comma and period look the same as in English.
